content.coreClaim: Power and knowledge produce each other. Discourse does not describe a pre-existing world; it brings its objects into being, and the authority to speak is itself one of power's rewards.
content.mechanism: Foucault's later work — The Archaeology of Knowledge (1969), Discipline and Punish (1975), and the lecture course on sexuality — moved from the episteme of his early period to power/knowledge: the claim that the two are not separate enterprises but one circuit. Knowledge is produced within relations of power — the clinic, the prison, the census — and power is exercised through knowledge: classifications, expertise, and the authority to name. A discourse is not just a way of talking; it is the set of rules that determines what can be said, by whom, and with what standing, and those rules have material consequences: diagnoses, sentences, admissions, budgets. The psychiatric category of lesson 1.3 did not merely describe patients; it called a population into being and organized an apparatus around it. This is why 'who speaks?' is always a question about power before it is a question about content.
content.canonicalExample: The American Medical Association's decision in June 2013 to classify obesity as a disease is a compact, documented case. Before the vote, obesity was a statistical risk factor and a moral condition — a matter of individual behavior. The reclassification changed the object: it became a pathology requiring clinical treatment, which reorganized insurance coverage, pharmaceutical research, clinical training, and the experience of millions of patients who now inhabit a medical category. The vote was contested precisely because it was not a discovery — no new mechanism was found in 2013 — but a redistribution of the power to name, with consequences flowing from the new name. Discourse made the object, and the object brought an economy with it.
content.conceptualTension: The critique of Foucault's account is usually political rather than empirical. If power is everywhere and knowledge is always its instrument, critics ask, then what grounds the critique itself — from where does one speak truth to a power that constitutes all truth? Foucault's answer, developed late, was that truth is not the opposite of power but a practice within it, and that critique works by mapping how particular regimes of truth function rather than by claiming to stand outside them. Whether that answer is sufficient is itself one of the live debates this curriculum keeps returning to.
content.connectionNode: Power/knowledge is the political completion of 1.3 (Episteme): the grid that organizes knowledge turns out to be maintained by institutions, not just inherited. It also gives 1.1 (Standpoint) its deepest sense — a standpoint is not only a location but a position within a regime that distributes the authority to speak.
content.microPraxis: Take a category that currently defines you — a diagnosis, a demographic, a classification in a system you use. Write the apparatus that produced the category: the committee, the criteria, the institution that administers it, and the year it was assembled. The category was assembled before it described you, and the assembly had authors.
content.zeigarnikHook: The authority to name is power's first instrument. Who named the categories you live inside, and what would it mean to renegotiate the names?

content.coreClaim: Modern power works less by punishing the body than by watching, measuring, and normalizing it. The Panopticon's genius is that subjects begin to govern themselves on behalf of the gaze.
content.mechanism: Foucault's Discipline and Punish (1975) reads the shift from spectacular execution to the prison as a change in the technology of power. The model is Bentham's Panopticon: a circular prison where a central tower can see every cell while the inmates can never see the watcher — so they must assume they are watched at all times. Power becomes continuous, automatic, and cheap, because the watched internalize the gaze and police themselves. Foucault's larger claim is that the prison is only the most literal instance: schools, hospitals, barracks, and factories spread the same logic of surveillance, examination, and normalization. The norm is the key instrument — the statistical average turned into a standard, against which every individual is measured and deviation becomes pathology. Modern power, on this account, does not mainly forbid; it produces — docile bodies that do not need to be forced because they have learned to force themselves.
content.canonicalExample: China's social credit system is the most literal descendant of the model. Announced as a national plan by the State Council in 2014 and piloted in dozens of cities through the late 2010s, the system aggregates behavioral data — financial, social, administrative — into scores that determine access to loans, trains, flights, and jobs. The details vary by locality and the rollout has been slower than its reputation, but the architecture is textbook panoptic: the score functions as a gaze that need not actually be watching at every moment, because subjects alter their behavior in anticipation of it. The system's most revealing feature is that it produces compliance through the possibility of observation — the Benthamite mechanism, running on databases instead of a tower.
content.conceptualTension: Foucault's account has been criticized from two directions. Historians argue the disciplinary society was never as total as the model suggests — coercion, spectacle, and sovereign force did not disappear, and Discipline and Punish overstates the replacement. Political theorists add that Foucault's analysis, by dissolving agency into normalization, leaves little vocabulary for resistance — a criticism he himself engaged late in his career, and which the abolitionist framework of 8.6 later takes up as its starting point.
content.connectionNode: Disciplinary power is the institutional machinery behind 3.6 (Cultural Hegemony): consent is not only ideological but produced through the everyday practice of being measured and compared. It also mechanizes what 1.1 (Standpoint) identified as the view from nowhere — the norm is a standpoint that has forgotten it is one.
content.microPraxis: List the metrics by which you currently measure yourself — steps, hours, grades, output, engagement. For each, name the norm it is quietly comparing you to, and the institution that benefits from the comparison. The list is the panopticon, and it is mostly voluntary.
content.zeigarnikHook: You have become the watcher of your own compliance. What would you have to stop measuring in order to notice who the measurement serves?

content.coreClaim: Modern power operates on life itself: birth rates, health, longevity, reproduction. The state manages populations as living beings, and the boundary where this management becomes violent is one of the sharpest questions in the field.
content.mechanism: Foucault's biopower, developed in the 1970s lectures and The History of Sexuality, names a shift in what power targets. Sovereign power operated on death — the right to kill. Biopower operates on life: it regulates populations through statistics, public health, demography, and the administration of reproduction, treating the population itself as a body to be optimized. Agamben's Homo Sacer (1995) pushed the analysis to its edge with the state of exception: the sovereign's power to suspend the law, producing a zone where some humans are stripped of political being — bare life — and can be killed without homicide or sacrificed without ritual. The critical note for this lesson insists on a distinction that is often blurred: Foucault's biopower and Agamben's state of exception are different frameworks with different lineages, and the relationship between them is itself debated. A short lesson cannot responsibly develop the sovereign/disciplinary/biopolitical distinction in full; what it can do is make the question precise: who is counted as a population to be fostered, and who as bare life to be exposed?
content.canonicalExample: The US Supreme Court's decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization (June 2022), overturning the constitutional right to abortion, is biopolitics in the most literal register: the state's administration of reproduction. The ruling transferred the regulation of pregnancy from individual decision to state legislatures, and the year that followed produced a documented patchwork — jurisdictions where gestational limits are enforced with criminal sanction, and jurisdictions where reproductive care is protected. What makes the case biopolitical rather than merely legal is that the object of regulation is not a crime but a bodily process, distributed across an entire population, managed through law, medicine, and surveillance. Whether one defends or opposes the ruling, the frame applies: life itself is the terrain of the contest.
content.conceptualTension: The conceptual tensions are as sharp as the political ones. Agamben's state of exception has been criticized for overgeneralization — applied to everything from immigration detention to pandemic lockdowns, the concept loses its edge — and feminist critics have argued that biopower's standard genealogies understate the specific history of reproduction as a site of gendered control. The syllabus flags the deeper issue: Foucault and Agamben are not the same theory, and treating them as one — as this lesson's own key-figures line invites — is a conflation the critical review asked us to mark, not to repeat.
content.connectionNode: Biopower is the population-scale form of the disciplinary norm of 4.2: where the panopticon watched individuals, biopower administers aggregates. Its machinery runs on the statistics and demography of 4.1 (Power/Knowledge), through which populations become governable, and it prepares the colonial extension in 4.4 (Necropolitics).
content.microPraxis: Take one public health or safety measure you have experienced — a screening program, a vaccination schedule, an insurance questionnaire. Ask which population it is designed to foster and which population it exposes. The question is not whether the measure is good; it is what kind of power it exercises.
content.zeigarnikHook: The same state that fosters one population's life can expose another's bare life. Where exactly does the line run — and who gets to draw it, using what instruments?

content.coreClaim: The ultimate expression of sovereignty is the power to decide who lives and who must die. Necropolitics extends the analysis of power into the colonial and postcolonial zones where death is administered as policy.
content.mechanism: Achille Mbembe's 'Necropolitics' (2003) argues that Foucault's biopower assumed a European horizon and missed the most revealing cases. Colonial power, Mbembe shows, did not mainly foster populations; it managed death — through slavery, conquest, and the creation of zones where inhabitants are treated as disposable. Necropolitics names this: sovereignty expressed as the capacity to dictate who may live and who must die, and the infrastructure that operationalizes the decision — borders, drones, occupation, camps, and the category of the enemy without rights. The concept's sharpest insight is spatial: necropower creates spaces of exception, colonial frontiers where the ordinary protections of law and life simply do not extend, and the line between war and peace, crime and policy, dissolves. Mbembe's question is not whether such power is cruel but how it is organized — what administrative rationality lets death become a routine procedure.
content.canonicalExample: The sinking of the fishing vessel Adriana off Pylos in June 2023 — in which around six hundred migrants, mostly from Pakistan, Syria, and Egypt, drowned while the Greek coast guard monitored the overcrowded boat for hours — is the concept's architecture made visible. The deaths were not a failure of rescue so much as the steady-state output of a system: a border regime in which the Mediterranean itself functions as a zone of exception, where the legal status of those crossing is suspended in advance and where the decision about who is saved is not an emergency but a policy parameter. The 2023 report by a European Parliament committee and the subsequent investigations did not find a malfunction; they found a routine. Necropolitics is the name for how such routines get built.
content.conceptualTension: The difficulty is the concept's tendency to totalize. If necropower is everywhere, critics ask, then it explains nothing in particular — and Mbembe's critics within African studies have argued that the concept, born from the plantation and the colony, needs careful calibration when applied to camps, borders, and occupations that have different histories. Its defenders reply that the calibration is exactly what the concept forces: the question is never 'is this necropolitics?' but 'which deaths are administered, through what apparatus, and who profits from the administration?'
content.connectionNode: Necropolitics is the colonial correction to 4.3 (Biopower): where biopolitics fosters life, necropolitics administers death, and the two run on the same statistical machinery described in 4.1. It also completes the physiological claim of 2.3 (Polyvagal Theory) — the populations cycling in the lower autonomic rungs are the ones necropower targets.
content.microPraxis: Take one week of news coverage. Count which deaths were treated as individual tragedies with names and biographies, and which were reported as numbers in aggregate. The ratio is not a fact about the deaths; it is a fact about the machinery that decides whose death is grievable.
content.zeigarnikHook: The line between policy and killing is drawn by administrative routine. What does it mean to be morally responsible for a death your government administers? And what would responsibility look like from inside the routine?

content.coreClaim: Capitalism did not become racist by accident. It emerged from and continuously requires racial hierarchies — race is not incidental to the system but one of its load-bearing structures.
content.mechanism: Cedric Robinson's Black Marxism (1983) argued against the standard story in which capitalism is a colorblind machine that racism merely distorts. Robinson's claim is that capitalism grew out of a feudal Europe already organized by racial difference, and that it has always depended on racialized labor regimes — plantation slavery was not a pre-capitalist relic but capitalism's formative laboratory. The modern phrasing, developed by Robinson's readers in Black Studies, is that capital needs difference to extract more cheaply: racial hierarchy supplies the justification and the sorting mechanism for differential wages, differential risk, and differential exposure. Ruth Wilson Gilmore's definition condenses the field: racism is 'the state-sanctioned or extralegal production and exploitation of group-differentiated vulnerability to premature death'. The point is not that race is 'really' about class, but that the two are fused — capital sorts bodies by race because the sorting is profitable.
content.canonicalExample: The Markup's 2021 investigation of mortgage pricing found that lenders charged Black applicants more than white applicants with the same financial profiles, in data covering millions of loans from the prior year — a finding that triggered federal scrutiny and Congressional hearings. What made the study significant was that it bypassed the historical narrative entirely: this was not redlining in 1937, but the algorithmic present, in which the pricing models themselves reproduced the disparity. The case shows the mechanism operating without any individual racist required: the sorting was embedded in the models, the data they were trained on, and the incentive to price risk by group. Racial capitalism, on this account, is not a set of attitudes but an architecture that keeps finding new technical forms.
content.conceptualTension: The contestation happens mainly at the edges. Some economists argue that disparities of the kind The Markup documented are explained by omitted variables rather than discrimination; the reply from its defenders is that the variables themselves — credit history, neighborhood, wealth — are products of the very history being bracketed. The deeper debate concerns strategy: if race and capitalism are fused, then remedies that only address one side of the fusion will reproduce the other.
content.connectionNode: Racial capitalism gives 4.1 (Power/Knowledge) its economic engine: the classifications that power/knowledge produces are also pricing mechanisms. It connects backward to 4.4 (Necropolitics) — group-differentiated vulnerability to premature death is necropolitics from the economic side — and forward to 4.6 (Coloniality), which follows the same structure into the global division of knowledge.
content.microPraxis: Pick one item you consumed today — coffee, clothing, electronics. Trace the racialized and globalized labor that made it cheap, down one real branch of the supply chain, as far as the trail will take you. The price you paid rests on an allocation of exposure and pay that you did not design but materially depend on.
content.zeigarnikHook: The system that prices your morning coffee also prices human difference. What would it mean to consume ethically — and is the category itself a way of not asking the question?

content.coreClaim: Colonialism did not end with independence; it mutated into coloniality — a global matrix of power that continues to organize labor, knowledge, and being around a Eurocentric center and its racialized periphery.
content.mechanism: Aníbal Quijano's concept of the coloniality of power, developed from the 1990s, distinguishes between colonialism — the historical administration of colonies — and coloniality — the pattern of power that outlived it. The pattern has three interlocking axes: the racialization of labor (the global division of work still maps onto the colonial color line), the control of knowledge (Eurocentric epistemologies installed as the only valid ones, with others demoted to folklore or data), and the coloniality of being (which lives count as fully human). Mignolo's later work on the geopolitics of knowledge sharpens the second axis: knowledge itself has a location, and the university, the canon, and the citation economy are part of the colonial matrix rather than neutral arbiters above it. The concept's force is that it explains continuity: why hierarchies reorganize rather than disappear when flags change.
content.canonicalExample: The Rhodes Must Fall movement is the concept's most visible eruption inside the knowledge apparatus itself. Beginning at the University of Cape Town in March 2015, students demanded the removal of a statue of Cecil Rhodes — the colonialist whose bequest funded the scholarships — and the campaign quickly expanded into a broader struggle over curriculum, hiring, and whose knowledge counts, spreading to Oxford and then worldwide. What the movement contested was not one statue but the matrix: an institution named, endowed, and epistemically oriented by colonial extraction, teaching a canon assembled under the same structure. Whether one agrees with every demand, the episode made the analytic point with unusual clarity — the colonial order did not end; it kept the keys to the university.
content.conceptualTension: Its critics press two questions. The first is empirical: if coloniality organizes everything, how do you measure its specific effects against other structures — class, state, gender — without making it an unfalsifiable master category? The second is strategic: the decolonial option of complete epistemic rupture has been criticized by those who argue the better response is reconstruction — using and remaking the existing apparatus rather than refusing it. Both debates are live within and around the decolonial literature.
content.connectionNode: Coloniality is the knowledge-regime counterpart of 4.5 (Racial Capitalism): that lesson followed the sorting of bodies, this one follows the sorting of knowledge. It also returns to 1.9 (Two-Eyed Seeing), whose relational epistemologies are precisely what the colonial matrix demoted — and what the decolonial option proposes to restore.
content.microPraxis: Look at the last ten things you read, cited, or were taught. Ask, for each: from which continents and which languages does this knowledge come, and whose knowledge is being treated as background or raw material? The geography of your citation is a map of the matrix, and it is not neutral.
content.zeigarnikHook: Your education handed you a canon assembled by a colonial structure. Which parts of what you know would you have to give up to know otherwise? And is giving up the only option?

content.coreClaim: Settler colonialism is not an event but a structure. Its logic is not primarily exploitation but elimination — the replacement of Indigenous peoples on their land — and the structure persists into the present, however peaceful the surface.
content.mechanism: Patrick Wolfe's famous formulation in 2006 — 'invasion is a structure, not an event' — distinguishes settler colonialism from other colonial forms. Where extractive colonialism aims to use native labor, settler colonialism aims to acquire native land and replace native society; its founding drive is elimination, carried out through whatever means the era permits — massacre, treaty, boarding school, assimilation, and, in the liberal present, recognition within frameworks the settler state itself defines. Glen Coulthard's Red Skin, White Masks (2014) develops the political consequence: because the structure persists, the settler state's offers of recognition and reconciliation tend to reproduce the structure rather than undo it, and Indigenous resurgence must therefore ground itself in Indigenous land and practice rather than in settler acknowledgement. The lesson's hard claim is that the past tense is a grammatical trick: the structure is not over; it is ongoing.
content.canonicalExample: Two dates bracket the claim's present tense. In 2016, the Standing Rock Sioux's resistance to the Dakota Access Pipeline — which the company had rerouted across the tribe's treaty land and water supply — gathered thousands and demonstrated that treaty obligations remain the live terrain of struggle, with the pipeline built anyway under a new administration. In October 2023, Australia's referendum on an Indigenous Voice to Parliament — a constitutionally enshrined advisory body — was defeated, with opponents arguing it did not go far enough and others that any constitutional recognition within the settler framework was itself the problem. Between the two events runs the argument Coulthard makes: the structure continues, and the question of whether to reform it from within or refuse it from without is not settled — it is the live question of the present.
content.conceptualTension: The strongest critics include Indigenous scholars themselves. Some argue the elimination/replacement binary flattens the enormous diversity of settler-colonial regimes and the different positions within them; others argue the emphasis on structural continuity can understate the real changes that legal and political victories have produced. Its defenders reply that the tests of the structure are empirical — land returns, treaty enforcement, sovereignty — and that the structure's persistence is measured by its ongoing effects, not by its self-description.
content.connectionNode: Settler colonialism is the land-specific form of the colonial matrix described in 4.6, and its elimination logic is the historical source of the group-differentiated vulnerability analyzed in 4.5. It also grounds 1.9 (Two-Eyed Seeing) in a political reality: relational epistemologies are not only different ways of knowing but live claims on land the structure is still organized to deny.
content.microPraxis: Find out whose land you are standing on, and one specific detail of how it was taken — a treaty, an act, a seizure, a border. Stay with the specificity until it stops being abstract. The point is not guilt but accuracy: the structure runs through the ground under your feet, and it is legible if you look.
content.zeigarnikHook: The structure of elimination is ongoing, and your own institutions sit on its land. What does it mean to say 'we' about the place you live, and who is entitled to decide?

content.coreClaim: Race, class, gender, and other axes of power do not add together; they multiply. Their intersection produces positions and forms of harm that single-axis analysis cannot see.
content.mechanism: Kimberlé Crenshaw coined the term in 1989 to name a recurring pattern in law: discrimination against Black women fell through the cracks of a framework that could see race or gender, but not their combination. The metaphor of the intersection is deliberately structural — it names where two axes of power cross, producing a position qualitatively distinct from either alone. Crenshaw later distinguished structural, political, and representational intersectionality: harms at the crossing, movements that organize along single axes and leave the crossing invisible, and images that erase it. Patricia Hill Collins extended the analysis from law to the matrix of domination: power operates on interlocking systems, and different individuals occupy different positions within the matrix depending on where their various axes place them. The framework's methodological demand is simple and severe: any analysis that uses a single axis — race, or class, or gender — to explain an outcome should be checked for what it is leaving at the crossing.
content.canonicalExample: The originating case predates the term by over a decade. In DeGraffenreid v. General Motors (1976), five Black women sued GM for a layoff policy that had never hired Black women before 1964 and laid off all Black women hired after 1970. The court dismissed the discrimination claim on the ground that the plaintiffs could not represent all women — since white women had not suffered the same harm — nor all Black people — since Black men had fared differently — and so their claim, being neither, was treated as being nothing. The case is the perfect exhibit because the court was not irrational: the single-axis categories were doing exactly what they were built to do, and the harm at the crossing simply had no name in the legal grammar. Crenshaw's 1989 article supplied the name.
content.conceptualTension: The internal debates are substantive. Some critics argue intersectionality, as institutionalized, tends to proliferate categories into identity rankings that lose the original structural point; others argue its emphasis on race and gender can underweight class — the oldest single-axis habit in the other direction. Collins and others have answered that intersectionality is not a taxonomy of identity but a method for analyzing power, and that abandoning the method returns analysis to the crossings-blindness that DeGraffenreid documents.
content.connectionNode: Intersectionality delivers on the promise of 1.1 (Standpoint): the knower at the crossing is precisely the one positioned to see what single-axis frameworks structurally miss. It also completes the sequence from 4.5 (Racial Capitalism) through 4.6 (Coloniality) — the axes this module has examined separately are shown here to operate fused.
content.microPraxis: Recall a situation you understood as a single-axis story — a workplace dispute, a political conflict, a personal history. Rewrite it with a second axis added: what changes at the crossing? The rewriting is the method; the habit of running it is the framework.
content.zeigarnikHook: Every single-axis story leaves something invisible at the crossing. What is currently invisible in the story you tell about your own life — and which axis are you using to keep it that way?

content.coreClaim: In the society of the spectacle, lived experience is displaced by its representation. The image precedes and generates the event, and authenticity itself becomes a manufactured commodity.
content.mechanism: Guy Debord's The Society of the Spectacle (1967) argued that capitalism had entered a phase in which social relations between people are mediated by images — 'everything that was directly lived has moved away into a representation'. The spectacle is not a collection of images but a social relation organized through images: the image does not report the event, it precedes it, so that the event is staged for its own mediation. Two of Debord's theses do the philosophical work: that the spectacle is the accumulated capital become image, and that what appears is good, what is good appears — appearance is the system's functioning principle. The consequence for critique: in a spectacular society, unmasking is not enough, because the system has already commodified the unmasking. The influencer documenting her authenticity is the spectacle's perfect figure — the performance of sincerity as a product.
content.canonicalExample: The collapse of FTX in November 2022 is the spectacle's own case study. The crypto exchange had built a vast image apparatus before it had a functioning business: Super Bowl advertisements, stadium naming rights, celebrity endorsements, a CEO photographed in cargo shorts and cultivated as a visionary who would give his fortune away. The image ran far ahead of the substance — the balance sheet was a fiction — and the fiction was the product. What the bankruptcy exposed was not fraud alone but a specific form of it: a company whose entire market value was the spectacle it projected, valued by investors who were valuing the image of valuation. Sam Bankman-Fried's trial and conviction in 2023 completed the arc: the spectacular figure, unmasked, became the spectacle again — the trial itself as media event.
content.conceptualTension: Debord's framework has limits its own era supplies. Critics note that the spectacle thesis, written for broadcast television, underdescribes the participatory character of platform media — the audience is not merely viewing the spectacle but producing it — and that the concept risks totalizing cynicism, leaving no room for the uses of images in organizing and testimony. The framework's defenders reply that the mechanisms shifted but the structure held: the image economy has only deepened, and the production of events for their representation is more, not less, total than in 1967.
content.connectionNode: The spectacle is the image-economy form of 4.2 (Disciplinary Society): where the panopticon normalized bodies, the spectacle normalizes appearances. It also anticipates 7.1 (Hyperreality), where the map/territory lesson of 1.4 is pushed to its extreme — the image stops representing the real and starts preceding it.
content.microPraxis: Notice one experience today that you are having partly for its representation — the photo, the status, the post it will become. Separate the experience from the image and ask which you actually want. The gap between them is the spectacle's signature, and its point of leverage.
content.zeigarnikHook: Authenticity has become a manufactured product. What would genuine experience look like, and how would you tell the difference from the inside?

content.coreClaim: The disciplinary society has given way to the society of control: power that is continuous, modulated, and algorithmic — operating not through enclosed institutions but through codes, scores, and permissions that follow us everywhere.
content.mechanism: Deleuze's 'Postscript on the Societies of Control' (1990) compressed the shift into a series of contrasts. The disciplinary societies Foucault described enclosed people in institutions — school, factory, prison — each with its own walls and routines. The societies of control run on networks: the corporation is no longer a factory but a flexible form that follows the worker; the prison gives way to electronic monitoring; the signature gives way to the password; the individual to the 'dividual' — the profile assembled from data fragments that track us across contexts. Control is continuous where discipline was intermittent, and modulation replaces the fixed standard: you are not normalized once, you are adjusted in real time. Deleuze wrote before the internet's consolidation, and the essay reads as its blueprint: identity verification, credit scoring, algorithmic adjustment of prices and exposure — power as a mobile calculation rather than a fixed architecture.
content.canonicalExample: The rise of remote-work surveillance between 2020 and 2023 is the concept's quietest and most total instance. With the shift to distributed work, employers deployed monitoring software — keystroke logging, screenshot capture, webcam checks, activity scoring — at scale, so that the disciplinary office was replaced by a continuous audit that followed the worker home. The 2022–2023 backlash, including Microsoft's own surveys showing a 'productivity paranoia' spiral — more monitoring producing more visible activity rather than more work — demonstrated both the mechanism and its absurdity. The worker in the monitored home is no longer enclosed in a factory; she is adjusted by a dashboard she cannot see, and the adjustment never pauses.
content.conceptualTension: The weak point is the essay's almost totalizing abstraction. Deleuze's essay, like much poststructuralist periodization, compresses messy empirical history into a clean before-and-after, and critics note that the disciplinary institutions — prisons above all — have not withered but expanded inside the society of control, so the two regimes coexist rather than succeed each other. The lesson's own honest position is that the postscript is a map of tendencies, not a chronicle — and the tendencies it mapped have, if anything, accelerated.
content.connectionNode: The society of control is the successor regime to 4.2 (Disciplinary Society), and its dividual profile is the population-statistics of 4.3 (Biopower) rendered per-person. It also supplies the infrastructure for 7.4 (Algorithmic Governance), where the codes and scores of control decide credit, bail, and benefits — and for 6.8 (Surveillance Capitalism), where the dividual is the product.
content.microPraxis: List the codes and permissions that gated your access today — phone unlock, bank login, platform sign-in, building pass, recommendation feed. Notice the moment you crossed each gate without thinking. The enclosure dissolved into a continuous surface, and the exercise is to feel the surface.
content.zeigarnikHook: Power no longer encloses you; it adjusts you continuously. Where is the outside? And is the last unmonitored place actually the inside of your own attention?
